clip-1.prompt: A 20-second widescreen high-speed race car chase through Banff National Park, rendered as photoreal animation. Use 16:9 framing, clear summer sunlight and natural colours. This is fictional CGI, not permitted public-road racing. Keep the red race car leading and the graphite race car pursuing; both have low bodies, rear wings and unmarked paint. The highway is winding, undivided and two lanes wide, with narrow shoulders. 0–5 s: A broad roadside view establishes both cars charging left to right through Banff's landscape. Hold jagged Rocky Mountain peaks sharply above dense pine forests; two open-water turquoise lakes occupy separate basins below the road. Bare rock and lingering summit snow rise above treeline. Engines grow from distant growls into fierce mechanical roars. 5–10 s: Cut to a low roadside tracking view. The graphite pursuer closes from three car lengths to one behind the red leader around a sweeping bend. Wheels spin rapidly; sunlight flashes across bodywork. Keep the turquoise water, pine-covered slopes and mountain skyline readable beyond the cars, with motion blur concentrated on nearby asphalt. Hear rising engine pitch, gear changes and rushing air. 10–13 s: A sharp dashboard insert inside the graphite car shows gloved hands making a small steering correction, the red car filling the windshield. No readable instruments. 13–17 s: Return to a broad roadside view as both accelerate uphill, the pursuer closing steadily. 17–20 s: A wide rear three-quarter view holds both cars half a car length apart beneath the peaks, lakes still visible beside the forest. Engine roars carry through the finish. No collision, other text, dialogue, music or subtitles.

brief: A 20-second widescreen high-speed race car chase through Banff National Park: two race cars tearing along the mountain highway, one hunting the other down. I want to see the mountains: the Rocky Mountain peaks, the turquoise lakes and the pine forests clearly visible.

queries: Banff National Park mountain highway scenery Bow Valley Parkway Icefields Parkway reference photos
Banff National Park turquoise lakes highway views Rocky Mountain peaks conifer forests
gate.why: The chase is invented, but Banff National Park is a real location whose highways, mountain peaks, lakes and forests require accurate visual references.

research.subject: Banff National Park race-car chase: factual and visual references. The Icefields Parkway beside Bow Lake provides a documented mountain-highway and turquoise-lake setting. No car models, drivers or historical period are specified, so their appearance remains undefined rather than invented.

looks.look: Parks Canada describes an unfenced, winding, undulating road only two lanes wide, with paved shoulders in some areas. Do not depict this roadway as a divided multilane motorway. ([pc.gc.ca](https://www.pc.gc.ca/pn-np/mtn/ours-bears/gestion-management/~/media/e90b27b17adc44858f5361a4cdd5d13b.ashx))

The tourism authority describes turquoise-blue water, surrounding glaciers and Bow Glacier high above the lake. Its page supplies separately labelled summer and winter reference photographs; these should not be treated as interchangeable seasonal appearances. ([banfflakelouise.com](https://www.banfflakelouise.com/experiences/bow-lake))

looks.thing: Rocky Mountain landscape along the Icefields Parkway
looks.look: Parks Canada's landscape description identifies jagged peaks, ice-draped ridges, forest-covered valleys and alpine meadows. These are documented regional features, not evidence that every feature appears together at every road bend. ([pc.gc.ca](https://www.pc.gc.ca/pn-np/mtn/ours-bears/gestion-management/~/media/e90b27b17adc44858f5361a4cdd5d13b.ashx))

The lower subalpine landscape has dense lodgepole-pine, Engelmann-spruce and subalpine-fir forests. Higher subalpine areas have spruce and fir interspersed with dwarf-shrub meadows and avalanche-path vegetation. Above treeline, the alpine landscape includes exposed rock, talus, moraines, snow and ice—not forest extending to every summit. ([parcs.canada.ca](https://www.parcs.canada.ca/pn-np/ab/banff/nature/environnement-environment/ecosystemes-ecosystems?utm_source=openai))

looks.thing: Herbert Lake and Mount Temple: additional roadside reference
looks.look: Parks Canada describes still water providing panoramic reflections of Main Range peaks, including Mount Temple. This supports a reflective mountain-lake look, but the source does not identify Herbert Lake as turquoise. ([parks.canada.ca](https://parks.canada.ca/pn-np/ab/banff/visit/les10-top10/glaciers-icefields.))

Parks Canada explains that the glacier once resembled a three-toed crow's foot; one toe has since melted and the middle toe is slowly disappearing. Do not restore a complete three-pronged shape merely to match its name. ([parks.canada.ca](https://parks.canada.ca/pn-np/ab/banff/visit/les10-top10/glaciers-icefields.))

facts.fact: The Icefields Parkway is Highway 93N, a 232-kilometre scenic mountain roadway connecting Lake Louise in Banff National Park with Jasper townsite in Jasper National Park. The full route is not entirely inside Banff; a Banff-only story must respect that distinction. ([parks.canada.ca](https://parks.canada.ca/pn-np/ab/banff/visit/promenadedesglaciers-icefieldsparkway?utm_source=openai))

Bow Lake is encountered along the Icefields Parkway, approximately 39 kilometres from Lake Louise. The tourism authority documents its turquoise water and Bow Glacier above it, making this a geographically supported reference for the brief's lake-and-highway setting. ([banfflakelouise.com](https://www.banfflakelouise.com/experiences/bow-lake))
facts.when: Present-day location; open-water appearance is seasonal

facts.fact: The Icefields Parkway's winter is long: Parks Canada says lakes turn white and trails remain covered in deep snow until mid-June. A clearly visible turquoise, open-water lake should not be presented as the normal winter appearance. ([parks.canada.ca](https://parks.canada.ca/pn-np/ab/banff/visit/les10-top10/glaciers-icefields.))
facts.when: Seasonal; Parks Canada's general description, not a guaranteed thaw date

facts.fact: Parks Canada's driving guidance gives maximum speeds of 90 km/h on major routes and 60 km/h on secondary roads unless otherwise posted. A chase exceeding the applicable posted limit must not be portrayed as ordinary permitted road use. ([parcs.canada.ca](https://www.parcs.canada.ca/pn-np/ab/banff/securite-safety/conduite-driving?utm_source=openai))
facts.when: Current published driving guidance; posted signs govern

facts.fact: Wildlife may be on or near any park road, and roadside fencing does not keep every animal off the roadway. The real setting cannot be assumed to be a wildlife-free racing corridor. ([parcs.canada.ca](https://www.parcs.canada.ca/pn-np/ab/banff/securite-safety/conduite-driving?utm_source=openai))

The eastern 17 kilometres of the Bow Valley Parkway have access restrictions. From March 1 through June 25, all travel is prohibited between 8 p.m. and 8 a.m. The published 2026 cycling-pilot periods restricting public vehicles were April 30–June 25 and September 1–October 6. Do not assume this alternative road is always open to cars. ([parks.canada.ca](https://parks.canada.ca/pn-np/ab/banff/visit/~/link.aspx?_id=352B6887FEA14F82B7BD516BCBB57049&_z=z))
facts.when: Annual nighttime restriction; cycling-pilot dates specifically for 2026

facts.fact: Commercial filming requires Parks Canada authorization appropriate to the project; applications must be submitted at least 20 business days before filming. Parks Canada may deny projects incompatible with visitor safety, visitor experience or park-management goals. A film permit must not be assumed to authorize a high-speed chase. ([parks.canada.ca](https://www.parks.canada.ca/pn-np/ab/banff/info/permis-permit?utm_source=openai))

Recreational drones are prohibited. Commercial drone filming requires both a Commercial Film Permit and a Restricted Activity Permit, and authorization is limited to specified management, safety, enforcement and related purposes. An aerial chase shot is therefore not an unrestricted filming option. ([parks.canada.ca](https://www.parks.canada.ca/pn-np/ab/banff/info/permis-permit?utm_source=openai))

story.style: 20-second photoreal animation in 2.39:1 widescreen; broad roadside views, sharp dashboard inserts, clear summer sunlight.
fact_use: The chase stays on the two-lane Icefields Parkway beside Bow Lake, within Banff National Park.
Bow Lake has turquoise open water in the summer setting.
Jagged Rocky Mountain peaks rise above conifer forests, with exposed rock and ice above treeline.
A posted 90 km/h limit and a 154 km/h speedometer reading explicitly establish illegal speeding.
Roadside wildlife remains a visible hazard.
story.story:
Summer sunlight fills a widescreen view of Bow Lake beside the Icefields Parkway in Banff National Park. Turquoise water stretches beneath jagged Rocky Mountain peaks. Dense lodgepole pines border the winding, two-lane road.

Red Seven, a red race car bearing 7, bursts into view. Blue Nine, a blue race car bearing 9, follows three lengths behind. Their engines rise into an overlapping roar.

A roadside sign flashes past: “MAXIMUM 90.” Red Seven’s digital speedometer reads “154 km/h.” In Red Seven’s rearview mirror, Blue Nine grows larger.

From the pine-lined shoulder, the view opens across Bow Lake again. Blue Nine closes to half a car length. Red Seven sweeps into a bend; Blue Nine follows the same tight line. Tires shriek against asphalt.

Bracken, a bull elk, stands among the lodgepole pines beside the next bend. Red Seven’s brake lights flare. Blue Nine’s brake lights flare a heartbeat later. The gap nearly vanishes.

The final wide view holds Bow Lake and the bare, ice-streaked peaks above the pines as both cars sweep past Bracken, their engines dropping to a ragged growl.
